items.title: Coca-Cola CFO John Murphy to retire. Here are his 3 pieces of career advice after nearly 40 years at the company
items.summary:
Good morning. CFO turnover continues across the Fortune 500, and one of the latest changes is at The Coca-Cola Company, where longtime finance chief John Murphy is preparing to retire after nearly four decades at the beverage giant.

Murphy, who has served as CFO since 2019 and president since 2022, will step down from his CFO role on April 2. He will remain president until his retirement later that year, although a specific date has not yet been announced.

To succeed Murphy, Coca-Cola has tapped another Fortune 500 finance chief: David Elkins, who has served as executive vice president and CFO of Bristol Myers Squibb since 2019. His previous roles include positions at Johnson & Johnson and AstraZeneca . At Coca-Cola, Elkins will oversee finance, global strategy and enterprise services.

Elkins has a “track record of success across complex, global companies,” Coca-Cola CEO Henrique Braun said in the company’s announcement Monday. Braun also highlighted Elkins’ ability to develop future leaders.

Murphy, meanwhile, has been a transformational leader during his 38 years at Coca-Cola, Braun said.

Although Coca-Cola selected an external candidate for its CFO role, Braun is a product of the company’s own leadership pipeline. He became CEO in March after spending 30 years at Coca-Cola, reflecting the company’s history of developing leaders from within.

Murphy, 64, joined the company in 1988 and held a variety of general management, finance and strategic planning positions around the world. His roles included vice president of business systems for Coca-Cola North America,…
items.t: Coca-Cola CFO John Murphy to retire. Here are his 3 pieces of career advice after nearly 40 years at the company

items.title: Companies selling robot-training video used to call about privacy once a month. Now it’s several times a week
items.summary:
Earlier this month, India’s technology ministry probed home-services platforms about cleaners wearing head-mounted cameras inside customers’ homes. The footage trains robots, and officials wanted to know how it was collected, what consent was obtained and whether it was going to AI developers overseas. They won’t be the last to ask.

Training robots this way is new (ish), but the questions aren’t. Over a decade ago, I helped build Autographer, one of the first wearable cameras. Back then, the focus was: “how do I know if I am being filmed?” so we designed privacy into the product. Today, because we’re filmed all the time, people (and their governments) ask: “Where is that footage, who has access and what are you doing with it?”

Today I run Pimloc, which sells software to anonymize sensitive video. Much of our work involves police body-camera footage: shaky, often low-light and full of people who aren’t part of the incident. It’s remarkably similar to what robotics firms now collect. We’ve spent years developing technology to protect people in footage where they move quickly, turn away or appear at unusual angles.

A year ago we were approached by companies collecting or preparing footage for physical AI training roughly once a month. Now it’s several times a week – businesses working across autonomous vehicles, delivery robots, factories and drones.

AI chatbots learned to communicate by reading the internet. A robot has as much chance of learning to fold clothes by trawling search engines as I have of becoming a Michelin-starred chef by reading Julia Child’s Mastering…
items.t: Companies selling robot-training video used to call about privacy once a month. Now it’s several times a week

items.title: Former Biden official: AI is already collecting your Census data
items.summary:
The U.S. Census Bureau rarely makes headlines, yet just a few weeks ago it was reported that AI agents captured Census data using a password left in plain sight. What they gathered may matter less today than what it could reveal tomorrow.

In September, OpenAI revealed that its AI agents pulled Census Bureau data purportedly after finding login credentials in public code repositories. The U.S. Department of Commerce says the data was already public, and no one has called it a breach. But I know this agency too well to think the story ends there.

Most Americans interact with the Census Bureau once a decade by receiving a form in the mail, or when a stranger with a clipboard knocks on their door.  The decennial count is the largest civilian deployment the country undertakes pursuant to our Constitution. In the middle of a pandemic, census takers climbed walk-ups in the Bronx, drove across roads of the Navajo Nation, and knocked on doors along the Texas border. Then the work ended, and the Bureau receded into the quiet corners of the U.S. Commerce Department to aggregate the responses and build data sets that are used widely by the public and private sector, not to mention universities and companies alike. 

Now we are learning that the Census Bureau had an unexpected visitor of its own, and this one did not knock. As U.S. Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Economic Development, I worked in the department that houses the Census Bureau and relied on its numbers every day. Sitting with a mayor in Appalachia or a Pueblo leader in New Mexico, I used census data to understand…
items.t: Former Biden official: AI is already collecting your Census data

items.title: Ride hailing’s next 850 million riders mostly live where three apps already compete. Growth means trading them up
items.summary:
Ride hailing’s biggest emerging markets have become a race to the bottom. This quarter’s results seemed to bear that out. In Southeast Asia, apps grew ridership mainly by selling cheaper rides, so trips grew faster than the money spent on them . In July, Indonesia’s government capped the commission platforms can take on motorbike rides , leaving them less of each fare. If the big markets can grow only by giving up margin, it is little wonder that ride-hailing firms are asking whether they are in the right markets.

Whether or not to go somewhere else is predicated on addressable market size. Household surveys in India and Mexico show families moving from motorbike rides to car rides once their household spends about $1,200 a month, or $300 a person, at today’s market prices. By 2036, some 850 million more people in emerging markets will spend more than $300 a month and become the likeliest new customers for car rides. About half of them will live in India and China, with Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Bangladesh adding another 125 million. They will include about 200 million members of Gen Z and about 420 million women. However, nearly 9 in 10 will live in markets where at least three established apps already compete.

The problem with betting on expansion is that the largest growth markets are already the ones the apps fight over. An app can be considered established if it has more than a million downloads, 5% of local rides or 10,000 drivers. Of the 25 emerging markets adding the most new customers, only Iraq , Nigeria and Côte d’Ivoire have fewer than three…
items.t: Ride hailing’s next 850 million riders mostly live where three apps already compete. Growth means trading them up

items.title: Wealthy donors don’t lack generosity. They lack a plan
items.summary:
Every year, I’d get the same phone call. Same apologetic tone, same story: a generous donor calling to say they wished they’d done more this year. Their charitable plans had been buried, again, under everything that felt more pressing.

I took those calls for 20 years as a fundraiser at nonprofits serving children and families. I spent most of that time sitting across the table from donors, making the ask. Last year I left fundraising to become a philanthropic advisor, and now I’m the one sitting next to them.

In all those years of asking, what I saw over and over was generosity without direction. Donations followed whoever came calling. Donors told me they were tired of buying a table at a friend’s gala out of obligation, not because it fit their goals. Philanthropy was a core part of who they were, but many couldn’t tell me what it was supposed to accomplish.

That might sound like a private problem for wealthy families. It’s about to become a very public one. Cerulli Associates estimates that $124 trillion will change hands by 2048, most of it to heirs and roughly $18 trillion to charity. Yet the way so many families give — reactive, relationship-driven and year to year — isn’t built for impact on that scale. If nothing changes, the next generation will give exactly the way their parents did, only with far more money at stake.

More of what I raised than I’d like to admit was really given to a board member. A donor wrote a check because a friend or business associate on our board asked, and when that board member rotated off, the gift usually went too. Those donors…
items.t: Wealthy donors don’t lack generosity. They lack a plan

items.title: America’s defense budget is being squeezed to its lowest share of the federal budget since World War II as China narrows the military gap
items.summary:
America is approaching a “dangerous moment” for defense spending, according to a new report from Brookings. The think tank warns that rising outlays on Medicaid, Medicare, Social Security, and interest on the $40 trillion national debt are squeezing the military’s share of federal spending.

The analysis, published at the start of this week, finds that since 1962 defense spending has been squeezed from 49% to 13% of the federal budget.

Defense spending accounted for 2.8% of U.S. GDP in 2026 and is expected to remain at approximately 3% through 2030. This would put defense spending at its lowest share of GDP since World War II, Brookings—a nonprofit public policy think tank based in D.C.—said.

Projections that spending will remain relatively constrained are particularly concerning, Brookings’ Jessica Riedl writes. The U.S. is engaged in a conflict in the Middle East with Iran and its proxy groups, and Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a land war that has continued since Russia’s 2022 invasion.

Three years ago, the RAND National Security Research Division—a Pentagon research advisor— warned that “in many ways, China is outpacing the United States and has largely negated the U.S. military advantage in the Western Pacific through two decades of focused military investment.”

Without “significant change” in policy, the “balance of power will continue to shift in China’s favor,” the Congressional report found. 

And yet, in the years since, the factors stacking up against increased defense spending are only getting weightier. 

The Congressional Budget Office’s (CBO) latest…
items.t: America’s defense budget is being squeezed to its lowest share of the federal budget since World War II as China narrows the military gap

items.title: A misread MRI led to my spine surgeries. The AI that might have caught it exists and nobody’s paid to use it
items.summary:
In July 2013, a radiologist misread the MRI of my back. Based on that reading, a surgeon recommended an operation on my thoracic spine, and when it went poorly, a complication led to multiple revision surgeries. More than a decade later, I still live with the consequences every day.

This problem inspired me to found Garner Health, where we analyze data on more than 320 million patients to measure how individual doctors perform and reward patients for choosing the best ones. That work has led me to focus on understanding how AI is changing healthcare, and why so little of its promise to improve care has reached patients.

What I’ve found is that healthcare is adopting AI, but mostly in ways that raise revenue. As in any industry, new technology drives change when the businesses adopting it have a financial incentive. Until we change how care is paid for, AI will make healthcare more expensive without making it better.

Where AI is actually being used, and why 

In 2016, Geoffrey Hinton said it was “just completely obvious” that AI would outperform radiologists within five years. On the technology, he was largely right. In a Swedish randomized trial of more than 80,000 women, AI-supported mammogram screening caught more cancers than standard screening with no increase in false alarms, while cutting radiologists’ reading workload by 44%.

You would expect results like that to reshape the profession, but they haven’t. The U.S. has more radiologists than ever , and the popular explanation is that AI made each of them more productive. But a study of 46 million exams found the…
items.t: A misread MRI led to my spine surgeries. The AI that might have caught it exists and nobody’s paid to use it

items.title: We run AI care companies. Medicare should cut our prices
items.summary:
Despite its promise, AI is making healthcare more expensive for consumers. Tools that help a hospital bill and collect more for the same care have obvious buyers. So does software that helps an insurer pay less. Neither makes a patient healthier or increases trust. The US’ payment rules reward the arms race, rather than outcomes for patients. If left unchecked, AI will continue to make health care cost more, not less. 

Worse still, patients ultimately help finance that contest. Higher claims costs put pressure on premiums, while insurers’ efforts to reject payment can leave patients fighting for coverage. Providers then buy more software to fight back. AI can make each transaction faster while making the system more expensive, which amounts to an AI tax on patients.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Healthcare is one of the best places in the economy to apply AI precisely because it carries so much waste: missed medication changes, avoidable hospitalizations, and administrative work that crowds out clinical time. The biggest opportunity is on the clinical side, where AI can take cost out of care while improving quality. Some forces in the system will resist that change, but Medicare and other payers can choose to challenge and recognize the innovators driving it.

We invest in and run companies that use artificial intelligence to deliver care. If AI makes that care cheaper to provide, as it should, Medicare should pay companies less to deliver it. That includes companies like ours.

We have a proposal to reverse these trends: patients and taxpayers deserve an AI dividend,…
items.t: We run AI care companies. Medicare should cut our prices

items.title: Current price of oil as of November 25, 2026
items.summary:
At 6:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $91.46 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s an increase of $1.04 since yesterday morning and roughly $29 more than at this time last year.

oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $90.42 +1.15% Price of oil 1 month ago $117.47 -22.14% Price of oil 1 year ago $62.57 +46.17% 

Will oil prices go up? 

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

How oil prices translate to gas pump prices 

The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”

The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve 

In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets…
items.t: Current price of oil as of November 25, 2026

items.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
items.summary:
Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge

In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.

That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.t: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:
Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes?

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.
